To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dietary treatment and length of supplementation had no effect on feedlot performance or carcass quality.
serum and adipose leptin concentrations were greater for heifers supplemented for 32 d with corn oil than heifers receiving rumen-protected CLA or the basal diet.

supplementation with corn oil or rumen- protected conjugated linolec acid for 32 d or 60 d during the final 60 d of the finishing period had no effect on feedlot performance or carcass quality of heifers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
effects of lipid supplementation from two dietary sources on serum and adipocyte leptin concentrations, feedlot performance, and carcasses of beef steers.

the effects of dietary supplementation with two sources of lipid (corn oil or rumen- protected conjugated linoleica acid) on serum and adipocyte concentrations of leptin in beef heifers during the last 32 or 59 d of the finishing period.
the effects of dietary supplementation with two different forms of lipid, corn oil and rumen-protected CLA, on feedlot performance and serum and adipose leptin concentrations in heifers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the addition of corn oil or rumen- protected conjugated linolec acid to the diets of feedlot heifers had little or no impact on feedlot performance or carcass characteristics.
the effects of supplemental rumen protected conjugated linolelic acid and corn oil on serum and adiposse tissue leptin concentrations were inconsistent.
serum concentrations of leptin were not related to performance or carcass quality in the current study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
serum leptin concentration does not appear to be an accurate indicator of body composition and/or performance.
serum and adipose leptin concentrations are affected by the length of time on feed, with serum leptin concentration increasing as time on feed increases.
serum leptin is not an indicator of performance or carcass quality in feedlot cattle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of dietary lipid supplementation to manipulate adipose tissue concentrations of leptin is not a practical approach to manipulate leptin concentrations in the serum of beef cattle.

the addition of dietary lipid, either as corn oil or rumen- protected conjugated linolec acid, did not affect feedlot performance or carcass traits, but increased leptin concentration in adipose tissue.
the addition of dietary fat to a finishing diet did not improve performance or carcass traits.
